Thank you, Chair. I have the honor to introduce amendment L.39 to draft resolution L.12 entitled "Question of Death Penalty" on behalf of the members of the Group of Arab States. These amendments pertain to Preambular Para 24, which currently reads, "Strongly deploring the fact that the use of the death penalty leads to violation of the human rights of the persons facing the death penalty and of other affected persons." Mr. President, The group expressed its serious concerns regarding the formulation of this paragraph, which asserts that the mere use of the death penalty leads to violation of human rights. Such a categorical statement does not accurately reflect international law, nor the current state of play of international legal jurisprudence pertaining to the use of death penalty. First, as enshrined in Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, there is no prohibition of the death penalty. Its use remain legally permissible under strict condition, including limitation to the most serious crimes, imposition only following a final judgment rendered by a competent court, full respect for due process and fair trial guarantees. A general assertion that the use of the death penalty systematically results in human rights violation is therefore inconsistent with the legal framework established under the ICCPR and risks misrepresenting the legal obligation of state parties. Second, while we acknowledge the growing international trend towards restriction or abolition of the death penalty, it remains a fact that international law permits retention of the death penalty under the aforementioned condition, and that it is the sovereign right of states to choose their legal penal code in accordance to their specific context and circumstances, and in line with their obligation under international law. The current language risks conveying a message of blanket condemnation, which may be interpreted as an attempt to delegitimize sovereign legal systems that apply to the death penalty in conformity with international obligation. In this context, the Arab Group proposed the following amendment to paragraph 24 to read strongly deploring the fact that the use of the death penalty could lead to violation of the human rights of the person facing the death penalty and of other affected persons. This revised formulation preserves the emphasis on human rights concerns in accordance with the stated objective of the resolution, while aligning the language with international legal norms and maintaining the neutrality and credibility of the resolution.

Mr. President, in Costa Rica, the death penalty was never a local institution. It was a colonial legacy. And I say that with all due respect, because as this delegation says year after year, in 1882, as part of our independence, President Tomas Guardia decided to abolish the death penalty, doing away once and for all with this colonialist past. 140 years have transpired since that day, and we are aware that overall, There are still some differing points of views about the death penalty, which is precisely why this draft resolution focuses on human rights, which is a universal principle. This year, one of the requests of this resolution looks at the most recent progress, strategies, best practices, and alternative approaches to reduce the scope of applicability of the death penalty and limit its use. The core group of proposing countries further decided to call for an analysis of the right to non-discrimination vis-a-vis the use of the death penalty, focusing on the multiple ways of discrimination, paying particular attention to social economic inequalities and racial discrimination, among others. Mr. President, during the negotiations, we listened with great attention and with much respect to all opinions, and we managed to make changes to this document so that we could have its current balanced version that maintains the spirit of the initiative intact, which is why I encourage all members of the Council to support this draft. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Algeria.

Thank you, Mr. President. Algeria has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993. In Algeria, the death penalty is only pronounced in a limited number of extreme and heinous crimes that gravely shock the public conscience, such as those involving the rape, torture, or killing of children. This carefully circumscribed application seeks to uphold public order, protect the most vulnerable, and prevent individuals from restoring to vigilant Justice, we firmly believe that any meaningful dialogue on death penalty must fully respect the cultural, legal, and societal context of each state. In this regard, Algeria advocates for a gradual, inclusive, and respectful approach to this complex issue, one that balances national sovereignty with constructive engagement and promotes understanding rather than imposition. On a matter of principle, Algeria also recalls that general comments issued by treaty Treaty bodies are non-binding and should be regarded as interpretative guidance rather than authoritative legal instrument. While we value the expertise of treaty bodies and welcome their contributions to human rights discourse, we reject any attempt to endorse or elevate these opinions to the level of binding obligations. In this context, Algeria considers that the proposed amendments bring much-needed balance, nuance, and legal accuracy to the text. These revisions allow for a more realistic and respectful approach that accommodates the diverse legal systems and perspective of member states. Accordingly, Algeria will support the amendments. Thank you.

Thank you. I don't see any other requests for the floor. I have been informed by the Secretariat that there are PBIs for this draft proposal, which amount to a total of $139,000. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Throughout the consideration of draft resolution L12, Indonesia has consistently underscored the need for a more balanced text, one that

respect the diversity of national legal system and domestic context and recognizes the absence of international consensus on capital punishment. We appreciate the core group's effort to bridge different views. However, we remain concerned with the exclusion of the proposal contained in amendment L.136, which reaffirms the sovereign right of all states to develop their own legal system. The L.136 amendment does not contest the universal nature of human rights, nor does it seek to exempt states from their international obligation Rather, it preserve the necessary balance between the promotion of human rights and the respect for national sovereignty. This balance lies at the heart of the United Nations. Without the inclusion of operative paragraph 1 bis as proposed, the draft resolution closes the door to a constructive discussion on the application of the death penalty. Mr. President, as a state party to the ICCPR, Indonesia has limited capital punishment to the most serious crimes in accordance to its national law, emphasizing on judicial discretion and safeguards. At the same time, Indonesia have observed A de facto moratorium on execution since 2016. In our new criminal code, scheduled to enter into force in December 2025, capital punishment is no longer a principal penalty. Death penalty will be a conditional and alternative punishment with possible commutation. Our national development showcases that it is both appropriate and necessary to recognize the prerogative of states to determine the pace and manner in which they address these issues in line with their specific legal, social, and cultural contexts. States must retain the sovereign right to determine their own criminal justice systems, including the application of the death penalty and any decision to establish a moratorium on executions. We therefore will vote in favor of amendment L.36 to bring greater balance and respect for national context and urge

others to do so.

Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Chile would like to address amendment L.36. Though state sovereignty is the very core of a modern state, its foundation lies in people. Sovereignty is not an end in of itself, but rather a means to protect dignity and the rights of those that comprise the political group. Over time, this concept has evolved, going from an absolute state-based notion to one that links it with responsibility. Today, sovereignty gains strength and becomes legitimate when it is used in order to protect human rights. From the lessons we drew from the Second World War, we understand that human right guarantees place limits on a state's behavior, even as regards events that take place within its borders. Human rights are just that. They're a limit to a state's power. They're a safeguard from potential arbitrariness. And with this understanding, my delegation rejects the proposal, for we deem it contrary to the spirit behind the creation of this council. To include a reference to sovereignty in this text would be tantamount to suggesting that domestic systems are above international obligations of states, or even that defining human rights standards on the use of the death penalty would constitute a violation of state sovereignty. This not only runs against the spirit of the resolution, but also against fundamental principles of international law. It is states themselves who, exercising their sovereignty, choose their actions by taking on international obligations in the area of human rights, which is why respecting human rights has never been foreign meddling. but rather following sovereignly accepted commitments by States, which also apply to those guilty of the most heinous crimes. Sir, during informal consultations, we heard time and again that international law does not prohibit the death penalty. This statement, though legally correct, does not recognize that Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights must be interpreted in the light of Article 31 of the Vienna Convention in good faith and in light of its purpose, the protection of the right to life, which is why any reference seeking to justify the use of capital punishment as part of a state exercising its sovereignty take steps away from the international standards that states themselves have accepted. It is unacceptable, then, that such a document comes from the Council.

As a member of the core group of this resolution, Belgium deeply regrets the introduction of this amendment, and this for the sixth time. We urge all members of the Council to vote against the proposed amendment, which is both unnecessary and misleading. The draft resolution already reaffirms the sovereign rights of states in its opening paragraph, in line with Article 2 of the UN Charter. The amendment, therefore, adds nothing new and risks undermining the resolution's core purpose, the protection of human rights in the context of the death penalty. This amendment seeks to polarize the debate, shifting focus from essential human rights concerns to a false dichotomy between abolitionist and retentionist positions. It mischaracterizes the resolution, which, as stated many times, does not challenge the legality of national penalties, but rather emphasizes the human rights obligations states must uphold, particularly under Article 6 of the ICCPR. Referring to national law as a shield against international scrutiny contradicts the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which prohibits invoking internal law to justify noncompliance with treaty obligations. Accepting this amendment would set a dangerous precedent, allowing similar language to dilute future resolutions on other issues. Moreover, the phrase in accordance with their international law obligations does not resolve the ambiguity. It opens the door to interpretations that national sovereignty can override human rights commitments, especially in the sensitive context of capital punishment. The resolution does not compel states to abolish the death penalty or alter their legal systems. It calls for respect for due process and procedural safeguards for those facing execution, upholding those standards is not a limitation of sovereignty, but a fulfillment of international legal duties. For these reasons, we strongly oppose amendment L.36 and call on all delegations to preserve the integrity of the resolution by voting against it. I thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. With deep sense of appreciation for the distinguished members of this Council, but also with a great deal of respect and speaking quite candidly, for Colombia it is not advisable to have amendment L.39, presented by the distinguished delegation of Algeria, representing the Arab Group, to the draft resolution L.12 on the death penalty. The paragraph which seeks to be amended has remained intact since it was first considered in 2015. It has never been amended to date. Changing its content now would mean watering down agreed-upon language that was carefully built in this Council. The amendment tries to relativize something that has been broadly documented. The use of the death penalty leads to the violations of the human rights of those sentenced and other people affected by it, among them the right to life, the right to a fair trial, the right to non-discrimination, including a racial discrimination, the right to equality before the courts, and the right to family life. And though the death penalty is not formally prohibited by international law, as we would hope and wish, its implementation is not compatible with the fundamental right to life. It must be said that the resolution does not assert that the death penalty is in and of itself a violation of human rights. What it does say, in no ambiguous terms, is that its use has led to and continues to lead to various documented violations in all regions. The term "leads to" in the indicative in the draft resolution is not really conditional at all. It shows a reality. Death penalty does lead to, not would lead to, consistent violations of human rights. And to say would lead to, could lead to, as proposed by the amendment, would unduly weaken the strength of the text and would obfuscate the facts, which is why we voted against Amendment L.39 and called on other members of the Council to reject it and to stand by their commitment for human rights and the inner consistency of this important text. Thank you.
Lord, the distinguished representative of France.

Thank you, Mr. President. France is proud to have contributed to the core group's draft, which is dense but always consistent on the death penalty, which took place during this session. You know that this topic is a priority. of France, which held which will hold the World Conference Against the Death Penalty in 2026. As Colombia said, there is no point in changing terms that have not been changed since this draft was first presented and to which no amendment was previously made. The death penalty is a violation of human rights of those who are convicted and of others close to them. As the representative of Chile said earlier, the framework defined by the ICCPR in Article 6 is of importance and we would like to refer to the High Commissioner's words in 2025, the death penalty is difficult to reconcile with human dignity. It can amount to cruel and degrading treatment. The death penalty is a violation of human rights which is cumulative, the first of which is the right to life, but also in many other frameworks, the right to due trial, non-discrimination with a gender perspective or equality before the courts. These violations were highlighted long ago by civil society, but also by the recent report of the UN Secretary-General. which was presented to this Council session. And this is the reason for which France calls to vote against this amendment and calls on other states to do likewise and to support the adoption of this resolution. Thank you.

This amendment tries to interpret the term more serious crimes only for the Human Rights Council and the UN Secretary-General. Using this approach denies that during decades, local courts, national courts, and regional courts, for example, the African Court of Human Rights and Peoples, have interpreted this term in an ongoing, consistent way within their own jurisprudence, that is, referring to very serious crimes such as intentional homicide. The amendment ignores this consolidated jurisprudence of courts from every corner of the world, the precise language of the resolution which underscores that more serious offenses be interpreted consistently and restrictively as if it were to apply exclusively to very, very serious crimes, which include intentional homicide. This does not try to impose one definition of more serious offenses. Far from it, actually. It simply wants to point out that its interpretation has been used consistently by courts from various legal systems over the world. Costa Rica, sir, will vote against Amendment L.58 and calls on all member states to vote a similar vote based on this explanation. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Romania.

Thank you, President. Romania fully supports draft resolution L.12 on the question of the death penalty and commends the Core Group for reintroducing this important initiative during the current session. The resolution is a valuable contribution to the ongoing global discussion on human rights, particularly through its emphasis on the principle of equality of arms. It highlights the need to prevent the arbitrary or discriminatory use of capital punishment, a non-negligible risk whenever fair trials guarantees are lacking. The steady global decline in the use of the death penalty reflects the impact of international legal instruments, such as the ICCPR, that permit capital punishment only in cases involving the most serious crimes. This threshold has played a key role in guiding countries towards moratoriums and increasingly full abolition. It has also helped define the direction of state obligations to gradually move away from this form of punishment. Despite this positive trend, we remain concerned by its continued application in cases that do not meet the required threshold of severity. This undermines both the spirit and the letter of international human rights law. In this context, Romania regrets the introduction of Amendment L58, which seeks to narrow the space for interpreting the term "most serious crimes." Rather than supporting the restrictive approach that has taken shape through years of legal reasoning and practice, the amendment seems to challenge it. This is especially concerning given the fact that for the last decades, courts of law at all levels have interpreted "most serious crimes" in a consistent manner to mean offenses of exceptional gravity involving intentional killing. "Consistently" does not mean "unanimously." While it is true that there is no universally agreed definition of the term "most serious crimes," Resolution L.12 does not attempt to impose one. The resolution simply recalls that the interpretation has been applied coherently and progressively across jurisdictions around the world. These restrictive interpretations reflect the ongoing global trend towards limiting the use of capital punishment. National jurisprudence increasingly supports the view that the death penalty should be reserved, if at all imposed, only for the gravest of crimes resulting in deliberate loss of life. Weakening this standard would compromise efforts to prevent the death penalty from being used unfairly and arbitrarily, particularly in contexts where due process cannot be fully guaranteed. For these reasons, Romania will vote against Amendment 58 and encourages all other member states to do the same.

Thank you. I don't see any other request for the floor. At the request of the delegation of Mexico, the Council will now proceed to a recorded vote on L.58. I ask the Secretary to open the voting machine, and I ask all delegations to register their vote. I ask delegations to check whether their vote is accurately reflected on the screen. If so, I ask the Secretariat to close the voting machine. The voting is now closed. The results of the recorded votes are as follows: 13 in favour, 25 against, 9 abstentions. I give the floor to Council members for explanations of votes before the vote on draft amendment L59. I give the floor to the representative of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President. The amendment before us seeks to remove a critical reference recalling that mandatory death sentences deny sentencing courts their judicial discretion. rendering them arbitrary and inconsistent with the right to a fair trial and the right to life. The Kingdom of the Netherlands firmly opposes this amendment. Judicial discretion lies at the heart of justice. It ensures that each case is examined based on its individual merits, taking into account the circumstances of the offense, the situation of the accused, and any mitigating factors. When the death penalty is imposed automatically, without allowing judges to weigh these elements, it ceases to be an act of rendering justice and becomes an arbitrary deprivation of life. The Human Rights Committee, in its General Comment No. 36, has made this clear, and I quote, "Mandatory death sentences that leave domestic courts with no discretion as to whether to impose the death penalty are arbitrary in nature and incompatible with Articles 6 and 14 of the ICCPR." The Committee was crystal clear. Judicial discretion is an indispensable safeguard against arbitrariness and a precondition for fairness. Mr. President, recent developments confirm this. As noted in the Secretary-General 's latest report, Malaysia's 2023 abolition of the mandatory death penalty and the subsequent re-sentencing of over 1,000 individuals show how judicial discretion strengthens due process and prevents injustice. During this year's high-level panel on the death penalty, judges and officials from across regions and legal systems, from Malaysia to Zimbabwe and Morocco, underscored the crucial role of the judiciary in ensuring that punishment fits both the crime and the offender, thereby avoiding irreversibly miscarriages of justice. Mr. President, deleting this reference, as this amendment seeks to do, would weaken the resolution and undermine established human rights law. The Kingdom of the Netherlands therefore urges all delegations to vote against this amendment and to uphold the text as drafted. Justice requires judgment, no automatism. Judicial discretion remains a vital safeguard of human dignity and the right to life. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you, Mr. President. My delegation will vote against amendment L.59 for two main reasons. First, the amendment seeks to limit the scope of indispensable safeguards to guarantee that universal rights be respected, such as the right to life and the guarantees of due process, which are protected by Articles 6 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, respectively. Considering personal circumstances, including mitigating factors, in addition to being recognized guarantees by the Human Rights Council, are also criteria used by international courts, which have been a consensus here and in the GA. Secondly, the amendment seeks to delete the reference to the compulsory death penalty, ignoring that this practice has been qualified as arbitrary and incompatible with human rights. The jurisprudence of the Human Rights Committee and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, among others, have pointed out that the capital punishment used automatically violates the right to a fair trial. Given that it is not considered mitigating or aggravating factors or the proportionality of the sentence, this lack of court discretion turns the process into a formal transaction without effective justice, and it deprives the defendant from factors that could take into consideration the proportionality of the sentence, and that's a violation of a fair trial. Also, in the high-level roundtable on the death penalty of February 2025 and the Secretary-General's report of August 2025 underscore the importance of legal discretion which allows judges to use alternative sentences and proportional sentences, thereby reducing the use of death penalty in practice. Therefore, singling out different sentences guarantees that though a crime might be punished with a death penalty, the judge can determine whether this is the most fitting sentence or perhaps another sentence is more fitting and proportional. respecting human rights, which is why my delegation will vote no to amendment L.59 and encourages all members of the Council to reject it. Thank you.

Thank you. I don't see any other requests for the floor. At the request of the delegation of Mexico, the Council will now proceed to a recorded vote on L.59. Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of a cross-regional group of 27 countries. The list will be uploaded to the extranet. At the outset, allow me to underscore three points of international law that this Council cannot ignore. First, International law does not prohibit the death penalty. There is no global consensus either for or against its use when applied in accordance with due process and judicial safeguards. Second, there is no universally agreed definition of the most serious crimes. The ICCPR is silent on this. and references to General Comment No. 36, while often repeated many times, remain non-binding. Third, every state retains the sovereign right to determine the appropriate penalties for the gravest crimes under its legal system, consistent with its international obligations. For many of our countries, the death penalty continues to play a legitimate role in protecting our societies and deterring the most serious offenses. Mr. President, the draft resolution disregards these principles. relying on non-binding interpretations and presenting them as international obligations. This mischaracterizes the law and fails to reflect the diversity of legal systems represented in this Council. Despite our constructive engagement and consultations, our concerns were not taken on board. The draft remains one-sided and cannot enjoy consensus. For these reasons, on behalf of 29 countries, including seven members of this Council, we call for a vote on draft resolution L12. Thank you.
Thank you. I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Mr. President, the issue of the death penalty is a legislative and judicial issue which fall within a nation's sovereignty, there is no consensus on abolition or retention of this punishment, or on the interpretation of the term most serious crimes. When considering the abolition or retention of various penalties, including the death penalty, one must take into full account the level of economic and social development, social system, historical and cultural context of various countries, or whether these penalties can better serve the best interests of the people and social stability. In China, the death penalty is retained, but strict control and caution are exercised in its application with rigorous review procedures as required by law. Mr. President, when discussing and adopting resolutions on the issue of death penalty, the Council should take an objective, impartial, and balanced approach by respecting the judicial sovereignty of all countries. In this regard, China echoes what was said by the ambassador of Singapore when he presented the amendments, that the HRC cannot impose the values and the opinions of certain states on others, with no respect to the actual state of international law nor the diversity of state practice. Unfortunately, despite China and many developing countries' active participation in the consultation and our constructive suggestions, The sponsors failed to take our views into account and did not really solve our concerns. Therefore, China supports the statements made by the representative of Kuwait on behalf of a group of countries and to ask for a vote on draft resolution L12, and we will vote against, and we also call on other members of the Council to vote against draft resolution L12. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Mr. President, there has never been a consensus within the international community regarding the death penalty. The resolutions of the Council and the General Assembly are clear on this point. and they have been adopted, reflecting a divergence of views on this matter. The issue of the death penalty must meet a number of requirements. We are in favour of its elimination if conditions are appropriate for that, and therefore we take up the proposals for its elimination or moratorium. This is indeed the direction in which we should move. However, in parallel, our country has always attempted to defend itself and conserve its legitimacy in the face of attempts to destroy the Cuban people, and we have always done this in full compliance with all legal requirements while complying with judicial procedures. The penalty of the death penalty is used in very exceptional cases in Cuba. For years, no one has been sentenced to death by any of our courts, and this has been the case since 2003. Nobody is on death row in Cuba currently, and we hope that in a relatively near future, we will be able to completely eliminate the death penalty. However, this must be accompanied by an end of attempts by the United States in its activities which harm us. In this way, we could move forward. Draft L.12 does not reflect Cuba's position, and we cannot accept it as it stands. This draft resolution does not recognize the sovereign right of each state to shape a judicial system as it sees fit. and this, of course, in taking into consideration its specific features, but also the provisions of international law. Thus, Cuba has voted in favour of amendments L.36, L.39 and L.58. Our delegation, however, will not participate in the vote relating to L.12. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ghana.

Thank you, Mr. President. We thank the sponsors of draft resolution L.12. We attach great importance to the fundamental right to life and human dignity. In accordance with our constitutional and legislative framework, we place strong emphasis on transparency and robust fair trial guarantees, ensuring equal access to justice for all. We have carefully reviewed draft resolution L12 and welcome the continued consideration by the Human Rights Council of the question of the death penalty, which remains an unsettled matter under international law. Mr. President, Ghana support constructive dialogue within the Human Rights Council and in other international fora towards a unified position for the abolishment of the death penalty for all ordinary crimes. In Ghana, our 1992 constitution retains the death penalty solely for the crime of treason. However, in a progressive effort towards abolition, legislative amendment introduced in 2023 replaced the death penalty for ordinary crimes with life sentence. This pivotal step effectively abolished the death penalty for ordinary crimes under Ghana's legal system and placed Ghana's laws in alignment with its international human rights commitment. I wish to underline that pending constitutional amendment on the application of the death penalty for the crime of treason, Ghana's constitution and laws provide critical safeguards to ensure the free and fair trial of all persons in accordance with their legal and human rights and the application of the rule of law. It is important to underscore, in this regard, that criminal procedure is jurisdiction-specific. Hence, it remains the sovereign right of all states to elaborate their own legal systems and to provide for appropriate penalties. In closing, my delegation wishes to stress the agreed principle that the implementation of recommendations in resolutions is the sovereign right of each country, recognizing the need to respect the various legal and constitutional context while ensuring conformity with universally recognized international human rights. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. We understand that this resolution highlights the importance of transparency when addressing the question of death penalty. From the perspective that this is not an ideological confrontation between abolitionist and retentionist states, Japan has participated constructively in the negotiations with the aim of ensuring that the resolution reflects both positions. In presenting our position, we consider that international law does not prohibit the use of death penalty by states as long as their actions are compliant with international human rights obligations, and that there is no universally accepted obligation under international human rights law to introduce a moratorium on the use of the death penalty. Japan's death penalty system complies with the requirements of the treaties Japan has concluded, with respect to death penalty, and Japan operates its system strictly and carefully in accordance with due process. Nevertheless, it is regretful that this draft resolution is strongly biased towards the abolition of the death penalty and a moratorium on its use. We therefore feel a need to reiterate that the question of whether to abolish the death penalty and to introduce moratorium on its use is a matter to be decided by each state with careful consideration of public opinion, the crime situation, and the criminal policy of the state concerned. Whether to maintain or abolish the death penalty is an important issue that concerns the very foundation of Japan's criminal justice system.

This issue should be carefully

considered from various perspectives, including the realization of justice in society and trends in public opinion. In Japan, there are diverse opinions on this issue among the public, and serious crimes continue to be committed. Therefore, it is difficult for Japan to abolish the death penalty at the present time. For these reasons, we cannot accept this resolution and will vote against it. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you. I don't see any other requests for the floor. At the request of the delegation of Kuwait, the Council will now proceed to a recorded vote on draft text L.12. The Council will now consider draft proposal L20 Rev.1 entitled Preventable Maternal Mortality and Morbidity and Human Rights. I give the floor to the representatives of New Zealand and Estonia to introduce the draft proposal. Colleagues,

Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of the core group composed of New Zealand, Estonia, and Colombia, I have the honor to introduce draft resolution L20 on preventable maternal mortality and morbidity and human rights. When the core group first brought this resolution to the Council, the maternal mortality rate was 239 women dying for every 100,000 live births worldwide. Through collective effort, countries have reduced this to 197. This is an improvement, but still a far cry from our commitment in the Sustainable Development Goals to reduce the maternal mortality rate to less than 70 deaths per 100,000 births. We must do more, which is why we and our 51 co-sponsors continue to call attention to this vital issue. Every preventable maternal death is one too many. Our resolution urges states to strengthen health systems, ensure access to essential services, and address the root causes of preventable deaths, including discrimination and harmful practices. This year, we have placed special emphasis on midwifery. Universal midwifery coverage could prevent more than two-thirds of maternal deaths, save millions of newborn lives, and ensure that women and girls everywhere receive safe, respectful, and rights-based maternal care. I would now like to give the floor to the Ambassador of Estonia, Ms. Rea Salsa-Odriffen.

Thank you, Ambassador. Mr. President, our countries come from different regions of the world with diverse legal systems, traditions, religions, and customs. This diversity underlines both the universal nature of preventable maternal mortality and morbidity and the need for a transversal, collaborative response from this Council. Negotiations on this resolution were conducted in constructive spirit, building on more than a decade of work since the first preventable maternal mortality and morbidity resolution was adopted in 2010. We sought to preserve agreed language, to integrate new evidence and good practice, and to ensure text reflects both continuity and progress. Despite the advances made, the reality remains stark. Progress in reducing maternal mortality has stalled globally, and too many women and girls still die from causes that are entirely preventable. That is why this resolution is not only timely, but urgent. The core group reiterates its commitment to work with all delegations and stakeholders to transform words into concrete action so that every woman, everywhere, can experience pregnancy and childbirth safely with dignity and respect. We therefore invite all delegations to support this important resolution and to adopt it by consensus. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you. I wish to inform the Council that written amendments L35, L52, and L53 have been withdrawn. I now give the floor to the representative of Algeria on behalf of the Group of Arab States to introduce written amendments L40, L41, and L42. I would kindly request the representative to introduce all amendments on the understanding that each amendment will be acted upon separately. You have five minutes, please.

Thank you, Chair. I have the honor to introduce, on behalf of the Group of Arab States, amendments L40, L41, and L42, aimed to address specific non-consensual language contained in the draft resolution L20 Rev.1 as orally revised entitled Preventable Maternal Mortality and Morbidity and Human Rights. Amendment L40 concerns Preambular paragraphs 15 and 26 and operative paragraph 12 and aims at replacing the references to the so-called right to bodily autonomy, which does not appear in any human rights treaty. Thank you, Mr. President. Ghana supports the broad objectives of draft resolution L20 Rev.1, presented by New Zealand, Colombia, and Estonia. Ghana commends their joint effort. We particularly welcome the focus of the resolution on respectful maternal care including midwifery models of care. We further join the cause to accelerate the elimination of preventable maternal mortality and morbidity. For us in Ghana, the elimination of preventable maternal mortality and morbidity... For us in Ghana, essential services such as health infrastructure, education, and social protection are critical to addressing maternal mortality, and morbidity, and remains a top priority. We, however, wish to make the following point. Firstly, we reiterate our previous calls on the Council to be mindful of the prevailing international consensus regarding the right to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical, mental, sexual, and reproductive health. As we have said before, The right to sexual and reproductive health education is grounded in universal human rights, including the right to education and to health, as established in numerous international agreements, such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Mr. President, secondly, as a member of the African Union, Ghana has subscribed to sexual and reproductive health education policy commitment, including the 2005 protocol to the African Charter on Human and People's Rights, commonly referred to as the Maputo Protocol. Our position, however, on comprehensive sexuality education is that it must be age appropriate, culturally sensitive, and in accordance with our national context. We are therefore deeply concerned that these important safeguards are not reflected in the present text. Furthermore, we stress that the right to bodily autonomy is neither intergovernmentally agreed nor recognized under international human rights law. Finally, my delegation wishes to stress the agreed principle that implementation of recommendation in resolution is the sovereign right of each country, recognizing the need to respect the various religious and ethical values as well as cultural backgrounds of people to ensure conformity with universally recognized international human rights law. With that in mind, Ghana is ready to join consensus.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Gambia wishes to place on record its position regarding the resolution entitled "Preventable Maternal Mortality and Morbidity and Human Rights." We thank the core group of states, New Zealand, Colombia, and Estonia, for their leadership and tireless efforts in advancing this important initiative. Reducing preventable maternal mortality remains both a national and global priority in view of its vital importance in promoting the health, dignity, and rights of women and girls. The Gambia strongly supports this objective and is pleased to join the consensus on this resolution. However, the Gambia has taken note of certain elements that were the subject of the proposed amendments by Algeria on behalf of the Arab group. We supported these amendments in recognition of the imperative that the text of the resolution reflect differing cultural context and societal values whilst preserving our shared goal of improving maternal health and eliminating preventable deaths among women and girls. In this regard, the Gambia disassociates itself from language that seeks to broaden the concept of sexual and reproductive rights beyond the scope of internationally agreed frameworks, particularly the Beijing Platform of Action and the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development. These include references to bodily autonomy and comprehensive sexuality education without regard to appropriate cultural and societal values. Furthermore, the Gambia reiterates that its understanding of the term gender refers exclusively to the biological attributes of male and female. Notwithstanding these reservations, the Gambia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to eliminating preventable maternal mortality and morbidity and to promoting the health and rights of women in line with our international obligations. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Ethiopia welcomes the tabling of draft resolution A/HRC/60/L.20/Rev.1 and extends its appreciation to the core group members for their leadership in bringing attention to the pressing issue of preventable maternal mortality and morbidity. Ethiopia recognizes maternal mortality as both a public health and human rights concern rooted in broader systemic inequalities. we reaffirm our strong commitment to eliminating preventable maternal death through inclusive, equitable, and sustainable approaches. In this regard, we support the resolution's call for greater investment in health systems, midwifery, and the protection of health workers, especially in fragile and resource-limited contexts. In recent years, Ethiopia has made notable progress in reducing maternal mortality through the expansion of primary health care services. the deployment of trained midwives across rural and underserved areas, and the promotion of community-based health insurance schemes. We continue to invest in health systems strengthening, particularly maternal and child health services, with an emphasis on equity, dignity, and respect for women and girls. We welcome the resolution's focus on the rights of women and girls in vulnerable situations and the need to address structural barriers to maternal health. We also commend its emphasis on international cooperation, resilient health systems, and the vital role of midwifery in achieving universal health coverage. However, Ethiopia wishes to place on record its reservation regarding specific references within the resolution, particularly those related to comprehensive sexuality education and certain formulations concerning sexual and reproductive health, while we acknowledge that these issues are part of ongoing international discourse and enjoy support from many member states, we underscore that such matters remain culturally sensitive and subject to national deliberation, societal values, and legal frameworks. Ethiopia underscores that global commitments must respect national contexts, sovereignty, and cultural values. We advocate for a balanced and inclusive approach that accommodates diverse perspectives in advancing the health, dignity, and rights of all women and girls. In conclusion, while noting our specific reservations, Ethiopia remains firmly committed to the core objectives of the resolution. In the spirit of constructive engagement and in support of the rights, dignity, and well-being of all women and girls, Ethiopia will therefore join the consensus on its adoption. I thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. We would like to thank New Zealand, Colombia and Estonia for having submitted this draft resolution to us, which addresses an extremely important topic. The protection of maternal health is crucial. Maternal mortality affects many vulnerable women living in rural zones, living in poverty, or victims of discrimination. These are women who at times do not have access to quality health services, or at times their access is very limited. Moreover, sexual and reproductive health sometimes is not accessible to all women, and the violence which they face exacerbates the problem. Internationally, therefore, it is essential to provide high-quality, accessible health care to all women. Bolivia, therefore, guarantees the enjoyment of the rights of sexual and reproductive health. through our legislation, but the importance of comprehensive sexual education and maternal health services and combating discrimination in those services are crucial as well. And we know that there is much that remains to be done. Reproductive health is a crucial tool for the well-being of women. and plays a crucial role for millions of women and young girls as it helps us fight exclusion and discrimination. Despite the cultural specificities or the traditions of each country, we believe that we nevertheless need to adopt a joint position to ensure that no woman is left behind, especially in countries that are subjected to economic blockades. These are issues relating not only to public health, but also to human rights, requiring a multi-party and multi-stakeholder and multi-faceted approach.
